content:
Numerous Dropbox users received emails from the cloud storage service notifying them that their accounts had been accessed without authorisation, constituting a security breach. The latest report indicates that approximately 5,000 accounts were affected, with around 1,500 accounts having files downloaded.

The root of the issue appears to be that Dropbox failed to carry out identity verification when attackers configured single sign-on (SSO) options through a third-party company……

Developer Yoni Levy shared the contents of the email he received on the X platform.

Other Dropbox users also reported receiving the same email, in which Dropbox attributed the incident to a problem with single sign-on (SSO) using Lenovo account IDs.

Dropbox pointed the finger at Lenovo's email verification process, but The Cybersec Guru noted that the bigger problem appears to lie with Dropbox itself, which did not require users to authenticate through their existing login method when adding SSO.

  • Reconnaissance and filtering: Attackers gather target email addresses (sources include leaked databases, LinkedIn, customer lists, etc.—email addresses are essentially public information).
  • Malicious IdP registration: The attacker registers a Lenovo ID using victim@example.com. Because Lenovo's verification steps are missing or can be bypassed, access to the victim's mailbox is not required. The display name is set to a throwaway name—one victim who successfully recovered their hijacked account discovered that the attacker had set it to the late NFL commentator "John Madden," which clearly reflects that these registrations are large-scale, low-cost operations.
  • Federated login: The attacker clicks "Continue with Lenovo account" on Dropbox. Lenovo's authorisation server issues a token, with the email claim matching the victim's Dropbox account.
  • Implicit account linking: Dropbox maps the email claim to the existing account and establishes a login session. No password entry is required, no additional verification, and no "Do you want to link this new identity?" confirmation prompt. From Dropbox's perspective, since a trusted IdP has vouched for the email address, it naturally accepts it.

9to5Mac commentary

Although Lenovo certainly had shortcomings in its email address verification, had Dropbox authenticated users before allowing logins from newly linked identities, the incident itself would not have caused any damage. Failing to do so is a serious oversight.

Dropbox has fixed the vulnerability and invalidated all sessions previously "authenticated" via Lenovo IDs.

If you have not yet enabled two-factor authentication for Dropbox, it is strongly recommended that you set it up immediately.
